Shabbos Parshas Mishpatim,

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section discusses the verses about the half-shekel, its connection to the sin of the Golden Calf, and its parallel in prayer.

translations.translation: "This they shall give, everyone who passes among those counted, a half-shekel of the holy shekel—twenty gerahs the shekel—a half-shekel as an offering to Hashem..."1
And it concludes2
"to make atonement for your souls."
And the maamar of Shabbos Parshas Mishpatim and Parshas Shekalim 5680
(printed in Pardes)3
questions the double expression of "half-shekel" in the verse,
which says "a half-shekel of the holy shekel,"
and then repeats "a half-shekel as an offering to Hashem."
Also, what is the meaning of "twenty gerahs the shekel,"
since one only needs to give a half-shekel?
It also questions the meaning of "to make atonement for your souls,"
and as it continues and explains there that the concept of the half-shekel is to atone for the sin of the Golden Calf4,
and it questions what is the virtue of the half-shekel that it is so capable of atoning for that sin.
And one may add to this
(as a comment in brief),
that the sin of the Golden Calf is a general sin, and it is the source and root of all sins, iniquities, and transgressions.
And as it is brought in the Gemara5
that at the time of the Giving of the Torah, their contamination ceased
(that the serpent had injected into Chavah),
and after the sin of the Golden Calf it returned6.
And although it did not return completely as it was before that7,
for even after the sin of the Golden Calf the concept of choice remained for the Jewish people,
"and in us You chose"8,
in the physical body which in its materiality resembles the bodies of the nations of the world9
(and see in the Gemara there10
"Why are the nations of the world contaminated..."),
nevertheless, the sin of the Golden Calf is the general sin,
and about it is written11
"And on the day I make My account"
(for every sin)
"I shall bring it to account..."
Therefore, an explanation is most needed as to what is the virtue of the half-shekel that atones for this sin.
And now, from this offering
(of the half-shekel)
they purchased the communal offerings for the entire year,
and the concept of offerings nowadays is the concept of prayer,
as our sages, of blessed memory, said12
"Prayers were instituted in place of the offerings,"
and from this it is understood
that the concept of the half-shekel also exists in the service of prayer.

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains the concept of prayer as being from a "heavy head," referring to the deficiency in the Shechinah and in the souls of Israel.

translations.translation: B)
And to understand all this, the maamar continues to explain13
the concept of prayer,
and brings on this the statement of our sages, of blessed memory14
"One should not stand to pray except from a heavy head."
And one may add to this,
based on what Tosafos says in Maseches Menachos15
that the language "one should not... except..." comes to exclude, meaning it is invalid after the fact.
And so is the simple explanation of the matter,
that "one should not stand to pray,"
meaning that the concept of prayer does not apply,
except from a heavy head.
And it brings on this the explanation of the Maggid of Mezeritch, his soul in Eden16
that the prayer should be about the heaviness in the head,
that when one prays about a deficiency, he should not pray about his own deficiency, but about the deficiency above,
for there is no deficiency below that does not have a deficiency above.
And he explains,
that the concept of the deficiency above is as our sages, of blessed memory, said17
"At a time when a person is distressed, what does the Shechinah say? As it were, 'My head is heavy upon Me, My arm is heavy upon Me,'"
for the Shechinah is the aspect of Malchus, which has ascents and descents, etc.
And this is the concept of the "heavy head" of the Shechinah,
and this is "one should not stand to pray except from a heavy head,"
meaning, about the heaviness and deficiency in the head.
And afterwards it brings the explanation of our master, the Alter Rebbe
(and so it is also in the discourse "Ein Omdin Lehispael" of my revered father-in-law, the Rebbe18)
that "head" refers to the souls of Israel.
"Israel is the head for Me,"
and in this there is the concept of "heavy head" caused by sins,
as it is written19
"For my iniquities have passed over my head; like a heavy burden, they are too heavy for me."
